questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: 'She ______ a decision to resign from the company.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. MAKE collocations: make a decision, make a mistake, make a profit, make progress, make an effort, make a suggestion. DO collocations: do homework, do business, do damage, do research, do exercise. These are frequent exam traps.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: 'The government plans to ______ action against tax evaders.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. TAKE collocations: take action, take steps, take measures, take a break, take a risk, take responsibility, take a photograph, take advantage. 'The government will take action against defaulters.'

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: 'After years of effort, the scientists ______ a breakthrough in cancer research.'
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'MAKE a breakthrough' is the standard collocation. Other MAKE collocations: make a breakthrough, make a discovery, make an invention, make progress, make an improvement. Note: 'achieve a breakthrough' also works in formal English, but 'made' is the primary standard choice for exams.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: 'The lawyer ______ a strong argument in favour of his client.'
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'MAKE an argument' or 'PRESENT an argument' are the standard collocations. Related: make a case (for), make a point, make a statement, make a proposal — all involve creating or presenting a formal communication.

questions.stem: Which is the correct collocation? 'I need to ______ some research before writing my report.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. DO collocations: do research, do homework, do a course, do business, do harm, do damage, do work, do exercise, do a favour. 'Conduct research' is also formal and correct. 'Make research' is a very common error (interference from other languages).

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: 'Heavy rainfall ______ widespread damage to the crops.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'CAUSE + damage/problems/harm/disruption' is the most formal standard collocation. 'Do damage' is also used (informal). 'Give damage' and 'make damage' are non-standard. Also: cause an accident, cause trouble, cause delays, cause concern.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: 'The team ______ a meeting to discuss the project timeline.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. HOLD collocations: hold a meeting, hold a conference, hold a press conference, hold a seminar, hold talks, hold an event. 'The company HELD a board meeting last Monday.' Note: 'have a meeting' is also acceptable in informal usage.

questions.stem: Which is the correct collocation? 'The new medicine ______ a significant improvement in the patient's condition.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'MAKE an improvement' is the standard collocation. Related: make progress, make gains, make advances. However, in passive: 'An improvement WAS MADE in the patient's condition.' 'Bring about an improvement' is also formal and correct.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: 'She ______ a speech at the annual day function.'
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'MAKE a speech' and 'GIVE a speech' are both standard. MAKE collocations for communication: make a speech, make an announcement, make a statement, make a comment, make a remark, make a suggestion. 'Spoke a speech' is redundant; 'told a speech' is incorrect.

B is correct — 'DO a mistake' is WRONG. The correct form is 'MAKE a mistake.' This is one of the most common English errors in India. Key distinction: MAKE (for creating something, for errors): make a mistake, make a decision, make a profit. DO (for tasks, activities): do homework, do exercise, do research. 'Do a mistake' is a very common learner error.
